title: Ryokan plays
hookLine: Ryokan plays hide and seek with village children till after dark
last: I WISH I COULD GIVE THE MOON.

cards: Late afternoon in a village. Children run up to an old monk with a begging bowl and shout his name, not for a blessing, but to ask him to play. He sets the bowl down.
They play ball, then hide and seek, and when it's his turn to hide he crawls into a pile of straw in a field and goes perfectly still. The children search. It gets dark.
They go home for supper and forget all about him. The next morning, the story goes, a farmer comes to move the straw and finds the monk still there. Shh, the monk whispers.

teach.h: VERSIONS DIFFER ON WHERE HE HID.
teach.b: Like the thief story, this is a story people tell about Ryokan. Versions differ on where he hid; the monk stays the same.

teach.h: PLAY AS A PLACE FOR PRACTICE.
teach.b: First, play as practice. Ryokan's poems, as they've come down to us, keep returning to children, to a ball, to a spring day that ends too soon. Tradition says he carried a cloth handball in his sleeve.
For him, playing doesn't seem to have been time stolen from practice. It was a place practice showed up: full attention, no score worth keeping, no reputation to protect. Second, still hiding.
Why stay all night? Some readers hear a holy fool, too simple to notice the game was over. Others hear faithfulness: he gave his word to the game, and kept it.
Others hear complete absorption, so present to hiding that nobody was left inside to give up. The story doesn't choose for you.

teach.h: A WEEK OF TEACHERS FROM JAPAN.
teach.b: Third, the week behind us, a week of teachers from Japan. Bassui asked who is hearing. Bankei pointed to the unborn mind, already here.

Basho heard the sound of water when a frog jumped into an old pond. Hakuin, blamed for a baby that wasn't his, said is that so, and taught the butter that melts. Ryokan gave away his clothes and kept the moon.
And today he's in the straw, still hiding, waiting for the children to come back.

how: Ryokan's poems about children and play are read in Zen communities and in Japanese schools and homes, and his story is told as a picture of practice that includes simple joy.

games.q: you're Ryokan, hidden in the straw. it's dark, and the children have gone quiet. what do you do?
o: go home; the game is over.
call out so they can find you.
games.why: in the story he stays put all night, and when the farmer finds him, he whispers: shh, the children will find me.

practice: Pick something small and playful, tapping a rhythm on your knee, balancing a pen on one finger, humming a tune, tossing a balled-up sock from hand to hand, and do it with your whole attention, the way a child does when nothing else exists.
When your mind starts grading how silly this is, notice that, and go back to playing.

wordCard.voice: Ryokan plays. The monk who hid in the straw for the children's game and was still hiding at dawn. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese kakurenbo: hide and seek, the children's game Ryokan stayed in all night.

carryVoice: Your line: still hiding. For Ryokan, play could be practice, too. I'll be here tomorrow.
